7.text:
Previously ..

• So far we have covered the first of the main themes
  of this course – Virtualization

• Virtualization allows many programs or processes to
  run at the same time by sharing the physical
  resources of the machine

• We have seen how to take a single physical CPU and
  turn it into multiple virtual CPUs

• We have also seen how to create the illusion of a
  large, private virtual memory for each process

7.title: Previously ..

7.text:
Introduction

• We now move on to the second of the main themes of this
   course – Concurrency

• Concurrency exists at the OS level between different
   processes executing at the same time

• Concurrency can also exist within a single process

    – Here we introduce a new abstraction for concurrency within a
        single process: the thread

    – A multi-threaded program or process has more than one point
        of execution

• Nowadays, with multi-core CPUs, different processes or
   threads may execute in parallel on different cores

                                                                                                                             3
7.title: Introduction

7.text:
Single- and Multi-threaded Processes

  • In a multi-threaded process, each thread runs independently
      and may call various functions

  • Thus, instead of a single stack within the address space, there
      will be one for each thread

                                                                                                                                4
7.title: Single- and Multi-threaded Processes

7.text:
Threads

• Each thread is very much like a separate process, except
   that they share the same address space and thus can
   access the same data

• A thread has

    – A program counter (PC) that is used to fetch the next instruction
        to be executed by that thread

    – A private set of registers for computation

• Thus, if there are two threads on a single processor, a
   threads’ context-switch must take place

• Even on a multi-core CPU, there are generally many more
   threads than there are cores

                                                                                                                             5

   need to switch the page table)

• Instead of saving state to a process control block (PCB),
   we need one or more thread control blocks (TCBs) to
   store the state of each thread

7.title: Uncontrolled Scheduling

7.text:
Uncontrolled Scheduling

• Each thread when running has its own private
  registers

• The registers are virtualized by the threads’
  context-switch code that saves and restores them

• What can happen in the previous code:

    – The code to increment counter has been run twice,
      but counter (which starts at 0), may only be equal to 1

    – The problem lies in the private registers

• What happen here is called a race condition

                                                                                                                           13
7.title: Uncontrolled Scheduling

7.text:
A Race Condition

• A Race Condition occurs when the results
  depend on the timing execution of the code

• It is caused by context switches that occur at
  untimely points in the execution

• Wrong results may be produced
• And…the computation is no longer

  deterministic

                                                                                                                           14
7.title: A Race Condition

7.text:
Critical Section and Mutual Exclusion

• If multiple threads executing a code section can
  result in a race condition, we call this code a critical
  section

• A critical section is a piece of code that accesses a
  shared variable, or more generally a shared resource,
  and must be executed by only one thread at a time

• This code needs to have a mutual exclusion property
• This property guarantees that if one thread is

  executing within the critical section, the others will
  be prevented from doing so

                                                                                                                           15
7.title: Critical Section and Mutual Exclusion

7.text:
Atomicity

• One way to guarantee mutual exclusion is to have more
   powerful instructions that execute in a single step, e.g. a
   single instruction to add a value to a memory location

• This would remove the possibility of an interrupt between
   actions

• When an interrupt occurs, either the instruction has not run
   at all, or it has run to completion – there is no in-between
   state

• Atomicity means “as a unit”, “all or none.”
• However … this is not possible for all cases, otherwise the

   instruction set will be slow and very large
• Synchronization primitives are thus introduced instead

                                                                                                                           16

7.text:
We will be using synchronization primitives
to turn short sequences of instructions into

          atomic blocks of execution
   But first we look at some thread APIs

8.text:
Locks

• Mechanism

    – acquired, i.e. exactly one thread holds the lock
    – available (free), i.e. no thread holds the lock

• A lock variable holds the state of the lock at any instant in
   time

• The name that the POSIX library uses for a lock is a mutex,
   as it is used to provide mutual exclusion between threads

• Next … how should we build a lock?

    – Can we build a purely software lock?
    – What hardware support is needed?
    – What OS support?

8.title: Locks

8.text:
Evaluating Lock Implementation

• Mutual Exclusion: the lock should prevent multiple threads
   from executing a critical section at the same time

• Absence of Deadlock: if two or more threads are trying to
   enter their critical sections, at least one will succeed

• Fairness: each thread trying to acquire the lock should get a
   fair chance at acquiring it

• Performance: the time overheads added by using the lock

    – Overhead of acquiring lock when if no other thread wants to
        free it

    – Overhead of acquiring lock when there is contention for the lock

8.text:
Controlling Interrupts

• This was an early approach to implementing locks

    – The OS ensures code inside the critical section is not
       interrupted, and thus executes as if it were atomic

    – void lock() { disableInterrupts(); }
    – void unlock() { enableInterrupts(); }

• This is a simple approach but has many disadvantages

    – It allows any thread to perform a privileged operation
       (turning interrupts on and off) which is very risky – the
       thread may not enable interrupts again

    – The approach does not work on multi-core or
       multiprocessors

What about Performance

• Spin-waiting wastes time waiting for another
  thread to release the lock

• On a single processor, the thread that holds the
  lock cannot even run (at least, not until a context
  switch occurs)!

• Thus, as we move forward and develop more
  sophisticated solutions, we should also consider
  ways to avoid this kind of waste

8.text:
Hardware Support for Locking

• Although there are purely software solutions to locking (e.g.
   Peterson’s algorithm), some hardware support can provide a
   simpler and better solution

• The hardware support generally takes the form of a primitive
   instruction that is guaranteed by the hardware to execute
   atomically

• Examples provided on different architectures include:

     – Test-and-Set
     – Compare-and-Swap
     – Fetch-and-Add
     – Load-Linked and Store-Conditional
     – etc.

                                                                                                                           12

8.text:
Test-and-Set

    (Hardware Support for Locking)

• A Test-and-Set instruction is added to support the creation
   of locks based on spin-wait

• It returns the old value in the location pointed to by ptr,
   and simultaneously updates the location to the new value

• The key is that this sequence of operations is performed
   atomically

 Next … how to use the Test-and-Set instruction to build a lock

Fetch-and-Add (3)

• When (myturn == turn) for a given thread, it is
  that thread’s turn to enter the critical section

• Unlock is accomplished simply by incrementing
  the turn such that the next waiting thread (if
  there is one) can now enter the critical section

• This method ensures progress for all threads
• Once a thread is assigned its ticket value, it will

  be scheduled at some point in the future
• In previous methods, no such guarantee existed

8.title: Fetch-and-Add (3)

8.text:
So Much Spinning

• Hardware-based locks are simple and they work, but … they are
   inefficient with so much spinning

• Threads can waste an entire time slice doing nothing but
   checking a value

    – If a context switch occurs in a critical section, the value will never
        change until another context switch occurs

• With N threads contending for a lock, N−1 time slices may be
   wasted

• How can we develop a lock that does not needlessly waste
   time spinning on the CPU?

• Hardware support alone cannot solve the problem – we’ll need
   OS support too!

                                                                                                                           23
8.title: So Much Spinning

8.text:
Yield (1)

• When a thread is going to spin, instead it gives up
  the CPU to another thread

• An operating system primitive yield() can be called
  when a thread wants to give up the CPU

• Yield ()

    – Moves the caller from the running state to the ready
      state

    – And thus allows another thread to run

                                                                                                                           24
8.title: Yield (1)

8.text:
Yield (2)

• What if there are many threads contending for a lock
   repeatedly?

• If one thread acquires the lock and is preempted before
   releasing it, the other N–1 threads will each call lock(),
   find the lock held, and yield the CPU

• Each of the N–1 threads will execute this run-and-yield
   pattern until the thread holding the lock gets to run again

• There are still plenty of waste cycles
• And … the starvation problem still exists with some cases

                                                                                                                           25
8.title: Yield (2)

8.text:
Using Queues: Sleep instead of Spin

• Explicitly exert some control over who gets to
  acquire the lock next

• To do this, we need a little more OS support, as
  well as a queue (keep track of which threads are
  waiting to enter the lock)

• For simplicity, Solaris’s support is considered

    – park() to put a calling thread to sleep
    – unpark(threadID) to wake a particular

• Put a caller to sleep if it tries to acquire a held
  lock and wakes it when the lock is free

                                                                                                                           26
8.title: Using Queues: Sleep instead of Spin

8.text:
Basic Idea

• Lock: A thread checks a lock

    – If free, takes the lock and enters the critical section
    – If not, sleeps in a queue – Someone else will give it

      the lock later on

• Unlock: A Thread unlocks the critical section

    – If the waiting queue is empty, releases the lock
    – If not, pass the lock to the next thread in the queue
    – The next thread will be woken up with the lock and

      can proceed into the critical section

Different OS, Different Support

• Linux provides something called a futex which
  is similar to the Solaris interface but provides
  a bit more in-kernel functionality

• Suppose first we have a single int buffer (i.e. MAX = 1)

10.text:
Resource Allocation

• Resource allocation is a common requirement in operating systems
• Many resources need to be allocated dynamically, e.g. memory,

   printers, etc.
• Resource allocation introduces the issues of:

     – Mutual Exclusion – when a resource can only be used by one
        process (or thread) at a time

     – Starvation – a process (or thread) may be “locked out” by other
        processes (or threads) and prevented from acquiring a resource

     – Deadlock – two or more processes (or threads) may wait infinitely
        for a resource held by the other

      In this lecture, we will use the term “process” rather than “thread”

                                                                                                                             3
10.title: Resource Allocation

10.text:
Deadlock

• A set of blocked processes each holding a

resource and waiting to acquire a resource

held by another process in the set

– Example

• Semaphores A and B, each initialized to 0

P0            P1

sem_wait(A);         sem_wait(B)

sem_post(B);         sem_post(A)

                                             4
10.title: Deadlock

10.text:
Deadlock Conditions

• Deadlock can arise if four conditions happen simultaneously

    – Mutual Exclusion: only one process at a time can use a resource
    – No Preemption: a resource can only be released voluntarily by

        the process holding it, after that process has completed its task
    – Hold and Wait: a process holding at least one resource is waiting

        to acquire additional resources held by other processes
    – Circular Wait: there exists a set {P0, P1, …, Pn} of waiting

        processes such that P0 is waiting for a resource that is held by P1,
        P1 is waiting for a resource that is held by P2, … , Pn–1 is waiting for
        a resource that is held by Pn, and Pn is waiting for a resource that
        is held by P0

                                                                                                                             5

Resources

• Resource types R1, R2, . . ., Rm

        CPU, memory space, I/O devices

• Each resource type Ri has Wi instances

• A resource can be utilized by each processes
  as follows:

– requested (acquiring)                 sem_wait(A);
– used (holding)

– released                              sem_post(A);

10.text:
Deadlock Management

• Deadlock Prevention

    – Design the system in such a way that deadlocks can never occur

• Deadlock Avoidance

    – Allow the possibility of deadlock but avoid it before it occurs

• Deadlock Detection and Recovery

    – Allow the possibility of deadlock, determine if deadlock has
        occurred and which processes and resources are involved

    – After detection, clear the problem, allow processes to complete
        and resources to be reused (may require terminating processes)

• Ignore the Problem

    – Pretend that deadlocks never occur (some systems do this)

                                                                                                                           12
10.title: Deadlock Management

10.text:
(1) Deadlock Prevention

Limit the ways, a request can be made to ensure
  that one of the four conditions for deadlock
                  does not happen.

                                                                                                                           13
10.title: (1) Deadlock Prevention

10.text:
Recall: Deadlock Conditions

• Mutual Exclusion: only one process at a time can use a resource

• No Preemption: a resource can only be released voluntarily by the
   process holding it, after that process has completed its task

• Hold and Wait: a process holding at least one resource is waiting to
   acquire additional resources held by other processes

• Circular Wait: there exists a set {P0, P1, …, Pn} of waiting processes
   such that P0 is waiting for a resource that is held by P1, P1 is waiting
   for a resource that is held by P2, … , Pn–1 is waiting for a resource
   that is held by Pn, and Pn is waiting for a resource that is held by P0

                                                                                                                           14
10.title: Recall: Deadlock Conditions

10.text:
Deadlock Prevention: Circular Wait

• Impose a total ordering of all resources types and
   require that each process requests resources in
   increasing order of resource type

• If a resource of type j is held, process can only request
   resources of types > j

    – Example: Semaphores A and B, each initialized to 1

P0            P1

sem_wait(A);  sem_wait(B)

sem_post(B);  sem_post(A)

– Example: The Dining Philosophers

     • Require that each philosopher requests forks in increasing order of
        fork number

                                                                            15

The Dining Philosophers
Dining Philosophers, Deadlock
Dining Philosophers, No Deadlock

10.text:
Deadlock Prevention: Hold and Wait

• Prevent this condition by acquiring all resources at
  once

• Use a semaphore “Prevention” to ensure that this is
  done atomically

         sem_wait(Prevention);
         sem_wait(R1); // acquire resource R1
         sem_wait(R2); // acquire resource R2
         ...
         sem_post(Prevention);

• This has the problem of low resource utilization and
  starvation is possible

                                                                                                                           19
10.title: Deadlock Prevention: Hold and Wait

10.text:
Deadlock Prevention: No Preemption

• If a process that holds some resources requests another
   resource that cannot be immediately allocated, then all
   resources currently held are released

• This can be done by using trylock() (or trywait() on
   semaphores) to acquire the second or subsequent
   resource

         do {
                sem_wait(R1); // acquire R1
                flag = sem_trywait(R2); // try to acquire R2
                if (flag != 0) { // failed to acquire R2
                       sem_post(R1); // release R1
                       yield(); // or random delay
                }

         } while (flag != 0)
         ...

                                                                                                                           20
10.title: Deadlock Prevention: No Preemption

10.text:
Deadlock Prevention: Mutual Exclusion

• We know this is difficult, because the code we
  wish to run does indeed have critical sections.

   – Some resources may be sharable and do not need
      mutual exclusion

   – Using wait-free locking

         • Not use explicit locking, there is called wait-free
           technique. (require powerful h/w instruction)

                                                                                                                           21
10.title: Deadlock Prevention: Mutual Exclusion

10.text:
(2) Deadlock Avoidance

• Requires that the system has some additional
   information available
    – The deadlock avoidance algorithm dynamically
      examines the resource allocation state to ensure that
      there can never be a circular wait condition
    – Resource allocation state is defined by the number of
      available and allocated resources, and the maximum
      demands of the processes
    – Simplest and most useful model requires that each
      process declare the maximum number of resources’
      instance of each type that it may need

                                                                                                                           22
10.title: (2) Deadlock Avoidance

10.text:
Safe, Unsafe, Deadlock State

• If a system is in safe
   state  no deadlocks

• If a system is in unsafe
   state  possibility of
   deadlock

• Avoidance  ensure
   that a system will never
   enter an unsafe state

                                                                                                                           23
10.title: Safe, Unsafe, Deadlock State

10.text:
Safe State

• When a process requests an available resource, system must
   decide if immediate allocation leaves the system in a safe state

    – A safe state if one where there exists a sequence <P1, P2, …, Pn> of
        all processes such that for each Pi, the resources that Pi can still
        request can be satisfied by currently available resources +
        resources held by all the Pj, with j < i

• That is:

    – If Pi resource needs are not immediately available, then Pi can wait
        until all Pj have finished

    – When all Pj have finished, Pi can obtain needed resources, execute,
        return allocated resources, and finish

    – When Pi is finished, Pi +1 can obtain its needed resources, and so on

                                                                                                                             24
10.title: Safe State

10.text:
Banker’s Algorithm

• Used for deadlock avoidance when there are multiple
   instances of each resource type

• Safety Algorithm

    – Used to check whether the system is in a safe state

• Resource Request Algorithm

    – Used to determine if a request can be granted

         • If requested resources are not available, process must wait
         • If requested resources are available, “pretend” to allocate

            them and check whether the system is in safe state
         • If unsafe, process must wait, and the old state is restored

                                                                                                                           25
10.title: Banker’s Algorithm

10.text:
Example

• Suppose there is a single resource type, with 10 instances

    – At a particular time, the resource allocation state is as follows:

    Allocation Max  Need Need =

P1  1  6            5  Max – Allocation

P2  1  5            4

P3  2  4            2  Available =

P4  4  7            3  2 instances

– If P4 asks for one more instance, does this lead to a safe or
   unsafe state?

– If P3 asks for one more instance, does this lead to a safe or
   unsafe state?

                                                                          26
10.title: Example

10.text:
Example

• If P4 asks for one more instance, does this lead to a safe or
   unsafe state?

    – “Pretend” to allocate request – the state changes to:

    Allocation Max  Need

P1  1  6            5     Available =

P2  1  5            4     1 instance

P3  2  4            2

P4  5  7            2

– The request from P4 is unsafe, as for all Pi, Needi > Available

– If all Pi request the number of instances they still need, deadlock
   will occur – therefore request is not granted

                                                                       27
10.title: Example

10.text:
Example

• If P3 asks for one more instance, does this lead to a safe or
   unsafe state?

    – “Pretend” to allocate request – the state changes to:

    Allocation Max  Need

P1  1  6            5     Available =

P2  1  5            4     1 instance

P3  3  4            1

P4  4  7            3

– If all Pi request the number of instances they still need, the
   sequence <P3, P2, P1, P4> satisfies safety requirement

– The request from P3 is safe – therefore request is granted

                                                                  28
10.title: Example

10.text:
Avoidance Graph

• Used for deadlock avoidance when there is only
  one instance of each resource type

    – Claim edge Pi → Rj represented by a dashed line
      indicates that process Pi may need a resource Rj

    – Claim edge converts to request edge when the process
      requests a resource

    – Request edge converts to an assignment(used) edge
      when the resource is allocated to the process

    – When a resource is released by a process, assignment
      edge reconverts to a claim edge

    – Resources must be claimed in advance

                                                                                                                           29

10.text:
Resource Allocation Graph

Safe State – No Cycle  Unsafe State – Cycle

A request can be granted only if converting the request edge

to an assignment edge does not result in a cycle in the graph

• Request by P1 for R2 can be granted
• Request by P2 for R2 cannot be granted

10.text:
(3) Deadlock Detection and Recovery

• Allow system to enter deadlock state

   – Instead of preventing or avoiding deadlock, we
      allow deadlock to occur

• Detection algorithm

   – Execute a deadlock detection algorithm
      periodically to check for deadlocks

• Recovery scheme

   – If there is a deadlock, take some action to recover

                                                                                                                           31
10.title: (3) Deadlock Detection and Recovery

10.text:
Wait-For Graph

• If only one instance of each resource type, we maintain a
   Wait-For graph

                                                   Nodes are processes
                                               Pi → Pj if Pi is waiting for Pj

              Resource Allocation Graph Corresponding Wait-For Graph

                                                                                                                           32
10.title: Wait-For Graph

10.text:
Deadlock Detection

• If only one instance of each resource type

    – Periodically invoke an algorithm that searches for a cycle in
       the Wait-For graph – if there is a cycle, there is a deadlock

    – An algorithm to detect a cycle in a graph requires O(n2)
       operations, where n is the number of vertices in the graph

• If multiple instances of each resource type, a more
   general algorithm is required

    – A general algorithm to detect deadlock requires O(mn2)
       operations, where m is the number of resources types and
       n is the number of processes

                                                                                                                           33
10.title: Deadlock Detection

10.text:
Deadlock Recovery

• Terminate all deadlocked processes, or
• Terminate one process at a time until the deadlock cycle is

   eliminated
• In which order should we choose to terminate?

    – Priority of the process
    – How long process has computed, and how much longer to

        completion
    – Resources the process has used
    – Resources process needs to complete
    – How many processes will need to be terminated?
    – Is process interactive or batch?

                                                                                                                           34
10.title: Deadlock Recovery

10.text:
Summary

• Concurrency exists between different processes and different
   threads of the same process

• Critical Sections (e.g. accessing shared resources or shared data)
   need to be executed with mutual exclusion

• Locks and Condition Variables may be used by threads for mutual
   exclusion and synchronization

• Semaphores may be used by threads or processes for mutual
   exclusion and synchronization

• Resource Allocation may lead to deadlock where two or more
   processes (or threads) may wait indefinitely for a resource held by
   the other

Devices, Ports, and Buses

• Devices include storage, transmission, HCI devices, etc.
• Ports are the connection point between an I/O device and

• Buses convey data between device and CPU, e.g. PCI bus or

          ▪ Memory Bus for fast access to memory

Typical Device

• A Device has

    – An Interface it presents to the system

         ▪ Simple devices may have just a few chips
         ▪ More complex devices may include a micro-controller CPU,

11.text:
Device Interface

• Device Registers: Status, Command, and Data

    – Status register contains information that can be read by the
        kernel, e.g. if device busy, command complete, device error

    – Command register can be written by the kernel
    – Data register(s) can be used for passing data in and getting data

        out

11.title: Device Interface

11.text:
Device Interaction

• There are two techniques that a processor can
  use to command and transfer data to a device

   – Use special I/O instructions for reading and
      writing the device registers, called port-based I/O

   – Use Memory-Mapped I/O

         ▪ The device-registers are mapped into the memory
           space of the kernel

         ▪ The kernel uses standard store and load instructions

   – Some kernels use both techniques

11.title: Device Interaction

11.text:
Memory-Mapped I/O

                                                                                                    12
11.title: Memory-Mapped I/O

11.text:
Device I/O Locations

• Example I/O Locations on PC

                                                                                                                           13
11.title: Device I/O Locations

11.text:
Typical I/O Protocol

• OS executes four simple steps

    1) Wait until device is not busy (test Status Register)
    2) Move data (to/from Data Register)
    3) Command the device (write command to Command

         Register)
    4) Wait until device done

                                                                                                                           14
11.title: Typical I/O Protocol

11.text:
Polling Technique

• The I/O protocol described previously uses a polling
   technique

• In both waiting steps (1 and 4) the kernel is repeatedly
   reading a status register

• Inefficient and Inconvenient

    – It wastes CPU time just waiting for the (potentially slow) device
        to complete its activity

    – Why not put the calling process to sleep and switch to another
        ready process?

    – In this way, we can better utilize the CPU

• This uses a technique called Interrupt

                                                                                                                           15
11.title: Polling Technique

11.text:
Interrupt Technique

• Without Interrupts

    – While OS is polling for Process 1, no process is doing useful work

• With Interrupts

     – Process 2 is executing while the disk transfers data for Process 1

                                                                                                                           16
11.title: Interrupt Technique

11.text:
Interrupt Technique

• Basic Concept

   1. The OS issues a device command on behalf of the calling
      process

   2. Put the calling process to sleep, and switch to another
      process

   3. When the device has completed the operation, it will raise
      a hardware interrupt, causing the CPU to jump into the OS
      at a pre-determined Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) or
      more simply an Interrupt Handler

   4. The ISR finishes the operation (e.g. by reading data) and
      wakes the process waiting for the I/O

                                                                                                                           17
11.title: Interrupt Technique

11.text:
Interrupt Controller

• Interrupt Vector Table

    – Contains the vector to ISRs
    – The table is written at boot time or when the device is ready

• Interrupt Priority Levels

    – Allow high priority interrupt to preempt a low priority interrupt

• Maskable Interrupts

    – The kernel can choose to ignore maskable interrupts
    – Non-maskable interrupts cannot be ignored

• Interrupts can also be used for exceptions (e.g. page faults)
   or software traps (system calls)

                                                                                                                           18
11.title: Interrupt Controller

11.text:
Interrupt Vector of Intel Pentium
              Processor

                                                                                                                  19
11.title: Interrupt Vector of Intel Pentium

11.text:
Example of Interrupt for VM Paging

• Interrupt raised when page fault occurs (vector 14 in
   the Intel example)

• ISR is called, puts the process that caused the fault to
   sleep and executes the page management software

• Context switch another process to execute
• Device Interrupt when the needed frame is completely

   copied from disk
• ISR for disk is called, completes the operation and

   wakes the interrupted process

                                                                                                                           20
11.title: Example of Interrupt for VM Paging

11.text:
Polling vs. Interrupt

• Interrupts allow for overlap of computation and I/O
• However, for fast devices, the cost of interrupt

   handling and context switching may be larger than the
   benefits interrupts provide
• Also a flood of interrupts may overload a system and
   lead it to “livelock”

    – In networks, a large stream of incoming packets may each
       generate an interrupt

    – The CPU is so busy handling interrupts that no process can
       execute

                                                                                                                           21
11.title: Polling vs. Interrupt

11.text:
Direct Memory Access (DMA)

• With Programmed I/O as previously described,
  the CPU writes the data to the device

• Many I/O operations require a lot of data
  movement from/to main memory

• DMA is a hardware module that it helps the CPU
  with data movement between main memory and
  I/O devices, like hard disks

• Bypasses CPU then transfer data directly between
  memory and I/O device

                                                                                                                           22
11.title: Direct Memory Access (DMA)

11.text:
Direct Memory Access

• Without DMA

    – While OS copies data for Process 1, no process is doing useful
        work

• With DMA

     – Process 2 is executing while the DMA copies data for Process 1

                                                                                                                           23
11.title: Direct Memory Access

11.text:
DMA Controller

• To transfer data to the device, the OS sends the
  command to DMA controller for initiating the
  data movement (e.g. source and destination
  address of data and the size)

• The OS is then finished with the transfer and
  another process may be executed

• When the DMA is complete, the DMA controller
  raises an interrupt, and the OS thus knows the
  transfer is complete

                                                                                                                           24
11.title: DMA Controller

11.text:
Kernel I/O Structure

                                                                                                 25
11.title: Kernel I/O Structure

11.text:
Software I/O Interface

• We need software in the OS that knows the details of
   how a particular device works

    – I/O devices vary widely in function and speed

• Device Driver

    – Make the kernel I/O subsystem look generic as much as
       possible and independent from hardware

    – No need to recompile the OS every time that the OS has a
       new device

    – Easier for OS developers and more benefit for hardware
       manufacturers

                                                                                                                           26
11.title: Software I/O Interface

11.text:
Example of File System Stack

• Kernel I/O subsystem provides only basic block read and write
   in the generic block layer for file system

• How to read and write a specific block is the work of driver

                                                                                                                           27
11.title: Example of File System Stack

11.text:
Characteristics of I/O Devices

• Data transfer mode (Character-stream or Block)
• Access method (Sequential or Random)
• Transfer schedule (Synchronous or Asynchronous)

  or (Blocking or Non-blocking)
• Sharing (Dedicated or Sharable)
• Device Speed (transfer rate, latency, or seek time)
• I/O Direction (read only, write only, or read-write)

                                                                                                                           28
11.title: Characteristics of I/O Devices

11.text:
MASS DATA STORAGE

                                                                                                                       29
11.title: MASS DATA STORAGE

11.text:
Introduction

• Hard Disk Drives have been the main form of persistent
   data storage for decades

• Kernel needs sophisticated algorithms to access the disk
• Storage Structure must be formed under OS

   management
• Disk Interface

    – Drive consists of a large number of sectors (usually 512-
       byte blocks), each of which can be read or written

    – Multi-sector operations are possible, but only a single
       sector operation is atomic

                                                                                                                           30
11.title: Introduction

11.text:
Disk Geometry

                                                                                        31
11.title: Disk Geometry

11.text:
Disk Geometry

• Disk platter is a flat circular hard surface on which data is
   stored by magnetic changes on both sides, each of which is
   called a Surface

• Spindle connects all disk platters together and it is rotated
   by motor whose rate is measured in rotations per minute
   (RPM)

• Head is attached with arm above each surface – that arm
   will move around the surface

• Track is a sub-circle of each surface and each track is
   divided into sectors – corresponding tracks on each surface
   form a Cylinder

                                                                                                                           32
11.title: Disk Geometry

11.text:
Disk Speed

• A sector or block is the smallest unit of transfer

               TI/O = Ttransfer + Tseek + Trotation

• Disk speed (TI/O) has two parts:

    – The Transfer Rate (Ttransfer)
    – The Positioning Time which consists of two factors

         ▪ The Seek time is the time to move the disk arm to the
            desired cylinder (Tseek)

         ▪ The Rotational Delay is the time to rotate the platter to the
            desired sector (Trotation)

                                                                                                                           33
11.title: Disk Speed

11.text:
Disk Scheduling Algorithms (1)

• FCFS (First Come, First Served): It is fair but does
  not give good performance

• SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First): It is fast but can
  result in starvation where requests with long seek
  times are never serviced

• SPTF (Shortest Positioning Time First ): On
  modern disks the rotational latency can be
  almost as significant as the seek time so SPTF
  considers both

                                                                                                                           34
11.title: Disk Scheduling Algorithms (1)

11.text:
Disk Scheduling Algorithms (2)

• SCAN: The head sweeps from the outer to inner track
   and then back to the outer, repeatedly – avoids the
   starvation problem, but middle tracks get more priority

• C-SCAN (Circle SCAN ): It is like the SCAN algorithm, but
   the head only sweeps in one direction, e.g. outer to
   inner and then resets to the outer – fairer to inner and
   outer tracks

• LOOK and C-LOOK: They are like SCAN and C-SCAN, but
   do not sweep the full width of the disk – the head
   moves only as far as the final requested block in each
   direction

                                                                                                                           35

Disk Management (1)

• Disk Formatting

    – Low-level formatting: divide the disk into sectors (usually
       512 bytes) each with header and trailer that contain a
       sector number and Error Correcting Code (ECC)

• Disk Partitioning: before using the disk, the OS needs
   to group the cylinders into one or more partitions

• Logical Formatting: the OS constructs a file system data
   structure including maps of free and allocated space

                                                                                                                           39
11.title: Disk Management (1)

11.text:
Disk Management (2)

• Boot sector

    – Bootstrap Program: most OS have a tiny bootstrap (boot
       loader) in the boot ROM that it loads a full bootstrap
       program into memory

    – It contains the code that understands the disk partitions

• Bad sectors

    – “No disk can be manufactured to 100% perfection”
    – Example of handling bad sectors

          ▪ Manually check bad sectors by using format or check disk
             command (chkdsk)

          ▪ Using ECC to automatically detect bad sectors by HDD controller

File System and Its Implementation

                                                                                                             1
12.title: Lecture 12

12.text:
Previously …

• We have looked at general I/O management in terms of
   Devices, Ports and Buses

• We have studied a typical I/O Device and compared
   alternative I/O Protocols

     – Polling, Interrupt and Direct Memory Access

• We have looked at Mass Data Storage, in particular Hard
   Disk Drives and different disk scheduling algorithms

• We now go on to look at the File System

                                                                                                                             2
12.title: Previously …

12.text:
Recall: File System Stack

                                                                                                          3
12.title: Recall: File System Stack

12.text:
Introduction

• Each level in the diagram uses the
  features of a lower level

    – Last time we discussed the I/O control
       (Device Drivers and ISR) and how data is
       transferred between Main Memory and
       Hard Disk Drive

• We now focus on the higher levels

    – First, how to abstract the file system and
       operate it at the logical file system level

    – Second, how to implement and manage
       the file system

                                                                                                                             4
12.title: Introduction

12.text:
Abstraction of the File System

• We use the concept of Files and Directories to abstract the
   File System

• The OS abstracts from the physical properties of data
   storage to define a logical storage unit, called a File

    – It is a linear array of bytes that the user can read and write

• A Directory is like a file, but contains a list of name pairs

    – Each pair is (user-readable name, low-level name) of a file or
        sub-directory – the low-level name is often called an inode
        number

    – By placing directories within other directories, users are able
        to build an arbitrary directory tree (or directory hierarchy)

                                                                                                                             5
12.title: Abstraction of the File System

12.text:
File Structure (1)

• Overview

    – All files must conform to file structures that the OS
       understands

         ▪ Example: executable file structure includes the location of
            first instruction

    – Some OSs impose and support a minimal file structure

         ▪ Linux treats all files as a sequence of bytes
         ▪ Application must includes code to understand file structure

    – Some OSs have many different file structures which are
       indicated by file types

         ▪ This needs more complicated file support

                                                                                                                             6
12.title: File Structure (1)

12.text:
Example of Executable File Structure

                                                                                                                         7
12.title: Example of Executable File Structure

12.text:
File Structure (2)

• File Attributes

– Name: Some OSs give special significance to names and particularly extensions
   (.exe or .txt etc.) in the user readable name

– Identifier: the unique tag or low-level name, usually a number (inode number)
   that is not user readable

– Type: text, executable, other binary, etc.

– Location: a pointer to the device where the file is stored

– Size, Protection or Permission, Time and Date, and Owner User ID

• File Types

– Windows uses a file extension to indicate the type of file

– Mac OS stores type in attribute

– Linux uses symbols to describe the type     file permissions,          Symbol  Meaning
                                              number of links,           -       Regular file
                                              owner name,                d       Directory
                                              owner group,               l       Link
                                              file size,                 c       Special file
                                              time of last modification  s       Socket
                                              file/directory name        p       Named pipe
                                                                         b       Block device

                                                                                               8
12.title: File Structure (2)

12.text:
File Structure (3)

• File Access Methods

    – Sequential Access

         ▪ Supports operations: read next, write next, rewind, and skip

    – Random Access (Direct Access)

         ▪ Can jump to any record n (relative to start) and read or write
            that record

         ▪ Supports operations: read n, write n, and jump to n

    – Indexed Access

         ▪ Requires an index file, pointing to the ordinary relative file
         ▪ Very large files may require a multi-tiered indexing scheme

                                                                                                                             9
12.title: File Structure (3)

12.text:
File Operations

• Create

    – First, a location must be found on the device for the file
    – Second, the detail must be record in the directory where

       the file is created

• Read or Write

    – Need a read pointer or write pointer to the record in the
       file where the next read or write is to take place

• Delete

    – Search the directory entries for the file name then release
       the file space and erase the directory entry

                                                                                                                           11
12.title: File Operations

12.text:
Directory Structure (1)

• One Level Directory  A single directory for
• Two Level Directory  all users
                       Cannot have the
                       same file name for
                       different users

                       Separate directory
                       for each user
                       No files in the
                       master file directory

                                               12
12.title: Directory Structure (1)

12.text:
Directory Structure (2)

• Tree Structured Directory

    – Access files with absolute pathnames or relative pathnames
    – Leads to concept of

        current directory, e.g.
        cd /spell/mail/prog
    – Efficient searching
    – Grouping capability

            ▪ Users can organize their
               directories according to
               their use

                                                                                                                           13
12.title: Directory Structure (2)

12.text:
Directory Structure (3)

• Acyclic Graph Directory

     – The same file may need to be accessed in more than one place in the
        directory structure

     – Use a special file type, called a link

            ▪ Hard link

                    – Multiple directory entries refer to the same file
                    – Valid only for ordinary files
                    – Need reference count in the file

                       control block of how many
                       directories refer to this file

            ▪ Symbolic link or Soft link

                    – Contains information about where
                       to find the linked file (pathname)

                    – What happen when the original file
                       is deleted or moved?

                                                                                                                           14
12.title: Directory Structure (3)

12.text:
Directory Structure (4)

• General Graph Directory

     – Soft link can also be used to link to a directory
     – Cycles can lead to infinite loop problems

            ▪ How do we guarantee no cycles?
            ▪ Every time a new link is added can use a cycle detection algorithm

                                                                                                                           15
12.title: Directory Structure (4)

12.text:
Directory Operations

• Make

      – When the directory is created, it is empty, except for two entries

             ▪ A reference to its parent directory, (“..” in Linux)
             ▪ A reference to itself ( “.” in Linux)

• Write

      – The OS does not usually allow writing to the directory entry directly
      – However, operations on files or subdirectories (e.g. create, rename, delete,

         etc.) involve updating the parent directory

• Read

      – Allows the directory entries to be read, where each entry shows the mapping
         of the user-readable name to the inode number, along with other details

• Delete

      – Is the directory empty? If not, return error or delete all files and subdirectories
         recursively (dangerous)

                                                                                                                           16
12.title: Directory Operations

12.text:
File System Implementation

• We have looked at the abstraction of a file system and its interface
• We now go on to look at the file system implementation

     – This involves implementing the files allocation methods and the data
        structure of directory implementation

• Before that …

     – The file system needs to store important information on the disk of
        various types:

            ▪ Boot Control Block – information needed by system to boot OS
            ▪ Volume Control Block – details of volume (partition)
            ▪ File Control Block (inode in Linux) – details about the file

     – The OS needs to create partitions and mount a file system before use

                                                                                                                           17
12.title: File System Implementation

12.text:
Partitions

• A file system usually contains at least one partition
• A disk can be separated into a number of partitions
• Some OSs support partitions across more than one disk

                                                                                                                           18
12.title: Partitions

12.text:
Mounting a File System

• A file system must be mounted before use – the basic idea is to combine
    multiple file systems into one large file system tree

• This requires the name of the storage device and partition containing the
    file system to mount and the location within the directory structure to
    attach the file system, called the mount point

Unmounted file system  Mounted at
                       mount point

                          /users

                                                                             19
12.title: Mounting a File System

12.text:
File Allocation Methods

• The file allocation method refers to how disk
  blocks are allocated for files

   – Contiguous Allocation
   – Linked Allocation
   – Indexed Allocation

         ▪ Linked Scheme
         ▪ Multilevel Index Scheme
         ▪ Combined Scheme

                                                                                                                           20
12.title: File Allocation Methods

12.text:
Contiguous Allocation

• Each file occupies a set of contiguous blocks

    – Advantages

          ▪ Simple – only need the start block
             number and number of blocks

          ▪ Best performance in most cases

    – Disadvantages

          ▪ Difficult to know file size at create
             time

          ▪ Over-estimation of the file's final
             size wastes disk space and
             increases external fragmentation

          ▪ Under-estimation may require that
             a file be moved if it grows beyond
             its originally allocated space

                                                                                                                           21
12.title: Contiguous Allocation

12.text:
Linked Allocation (1)

• Each file is a linked list of blocks that are scattered on the disk,
   where each block contains a pointer to the next block

    – Advantages

          ▪ No external fragmentation
          ▪ Does not require pre-known file sizes
          ▪ Allows files to grow dynamically at any

             time

    – Disadvantages

          ▪ Only efficient for sequential access files
          ▪ Space wasted by pointers
          ▪ Allocating clusters of blocks reduces the

             wasted space, at the cost of internal
             fragmentation

                                                                                                                           22
12.title: Linked Allocation (1)

12.text:
Linked Allocation (2)

• The File Allocation Table (FAT) is a variation of linked
   allocation, where all the links are stored in a
   separate table at the beginning of the partition

    – The directory contains the first block of file,
        used to index the FAT

    – Advantage

          ▪ FAT can be cached in Main Memory for more
             efficiency

                                                                                                                           23
12.title: Linked Allocation (2)

12.text:
Indexed Allocation

• This combines all of the block numbers for accessing each file
   into a special index block (for that file)

    – Advantages

          ▪ Allows random (direct) access
             without external fragmentation

    – Disadvantages

          ▪ Some disk space is wasted
             because an entire index block
             must be allocated for each file

    – How should the index be
        implemented?

            ▪ How can we support large files that
               need more than one index block?

                                                                                                                           24
12.title: Indexed Allocation

12.text:
Index Block Implementation (1)

• Linked Scheme

     – The first index block contains header information, the first set of block
        numbers, and if necessary a pointer to additional linked index blocks

• Multilevel Index Scheme

     – The first index block contains a set of pointers to secondary index
        blocks, which in turn contain pointers to the actual data blocks

     – May have more than one level of indirect index blocks

• Combined Scheme

     – This is the scheme used in UNIX/Linux inodes
     – The first 12 or so data block pointers are stored directly in the inode
     – Then single, double, and triple indirect pointers provide access to

        more data blocks as needed

                                                                                                                           25
12.title: Index Block Implementation (1)

12.text:
Index Block Implementation (2)

• Combined Scheme (continued)

                               • For small files (which many are),
                                  the data blocks are readily
                                  accessible

                               • Medium size files are accessible
                                  with only a single indirect index
                                  block

                               • Huge files are still accessible using a
                                  relatively small number of disk
                                  accesses

                                                                          26
12.title: Index Block Implementation (2)

12.text:
File Allocation Performance

• The best method is different for sequential access than for random
   access, and is also different for small files than for large files

     – Contiguous allocation is good for sequential and random access, but
        has disadvantages, especially when the size is unknown at create time

     – Linked allocation is good for sequential, but not for random access

• Some OSs require specifying how the file is to be used at create
   time

     – Use linked allocation for sequential access and contiguous or indexed
        allocation for random access

• Some OSs automatically switch their allocation method

     – Use contiguous allocation for small files, and automatically switch to
        indexed allocation when the file size exceeds a threshold

                                                                                                                           27
12.title: File Allocation Performance

12.text:
Data Structure of Directory
              Implementation

• Directories need fast search, insert, and delete operations, with a
   minimum of wasted disk space

     – Linear List

            ▪ A linear list of file names with corresponding inode number
            ▪ Simplest and easiest directory structure to set up, but finding a file requires a

                linear search
            ▪ Sorting the list makes searching faster, at the expense of more complex

               insertions and deletions
            ▪ A linked list makes insertions and deletions into a sorted list easier, with an

                overhead for the links
            ▪ More complex data structures, such as B-trees, could also be considered

     – Hash Table

            ▪ A hash table can be used to speed up searching
            ▪ Collisions need to be handled, e.g. chained-overflow method

                                                                                                                           29
12.title: Data Structure of Directory

12.text:
Journaling File System

• A Journaling (Log Based) file system records each update to the file
   system as a transaction (set of changes)

• All transactions are first written to a log (separate device or section
   of disk)

     – A transaction is considered committed once it is written to the log
     – However, the file system may not yet be updated

• The transactions in the log are asynchronously written to the file
   system structures

     – After the file system structures are updated, the transaction is
        removed from the log

• If the system crashes, all remaining transactions in the log must still
   be performed

     – Faster recovery from crash, removes chance of inconsistency

                                                                                                                           31
12.title: Journaling File System

12.text:
Redundant Array of Independent Disks

• Redundant Array of Independent (Inexpensive) Disks

     – The idea is to employ a group of hard disks together with some form
        of duplication, either to increase reliability or to speed up operations,
        or both

• Improvement of Reliability via Redundancy

     – Mirroring, in which a system stores identical data on two or more disks

• Improvement in Performance via Parallelism

     – Striping, where data out is spread across multiple disks that can be
        accessed simultaneously

            ▪ Bit-level striping – bits of each byte are striped across multiple disks
            ▪ Block-level striping – data is spread across multiple disks block-by-block

• There are a number of different schemes that combine mirroring
   and striping

                                                                                                                           32
12.title: Redundant Array of Independent Disks

12.text:
RAID Level

Level 0: Striping, no mirroring
Level 1: Mirroring, no striping
Level 2: Error-correcting code (ECC) on

         additional disks instead of mirroring
Level 3: Bit-striping and dedicated parity disk
Level 4: Block-striping and dedicated parity

         disk
Level 5: Block-striping with rotating parity

         bits (the same disk cannot hold both
         data and parity for the same block)
Level 6: Block-striping with dual rotating
         parities, can handle two disk failures

                                                                                                                              33
12.title: RAID Level

12.text:
Combined RAID Levels

Also two RAID levels that combine levels
0 and 1 in different ways:
RAID level 0+1: disks are first striped, and
then mirrored to another set
A single disk failure will wipe out one
stripe set, but the other set can still be
used – cannot handle two disk failures
RAID level 1+0: disks are mirrored in
pairs, and then striped
Can handle as many as four disk failures,
as long as no two of them are in the same
mirror pair

                                                                                                                           34
12.title: Combined RAID Levels
